📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When running a high-traffic bilingual (Arabic RTL / English LTR) Laravel 11 application serving enterprise B2B portals and diagnostic tools, server response time (TTFB — Time to First Byte) directly dictates both Core Web Vitals (LCP) and search engine crawl efficiency.

Here is the exact production engineering checklist our team at MTM4WEB used to bring median TTFB down from 1,277ms (with 9s spikes) to 60–120ms on a live Nginx + PHP 8.3-FPM stack.

On many HestiaCP / cPanel reverse-proxy setups, static files inside public_html/public accidentally pass through a rewrite or backend hop if the Nginx location block doesn't resolve the /public root directly.

Serving static assets (.css, .js, .webp, .woff2) directly from Nginx with long immutable cache headers eliminates unnecessary backend worker contention:.

When pm = ondemand is used with a low pm.max_children = 5, concurrent bursts (especially when search engine crawlers and consumers hit the site simultaneously) force requests to queue while FPM forks upcoming children.

Switching to a warm dynamic pool keeps workers ready in RAM:.

Never leave production running uncached configuration or debug listeners:.

Combined with PHP 8.3 OPcache (opcache.enable=1, opcache.memory_consumption=256), route resolution and config lookup drop to single-digit milliseconds.

If your application logs visitor analytics to MySQL on every request via middleware, bots probing 404 URLs or polling AJAX endpoints will flood your database with synchronous INSERT queries. Guard your middleware so it only logs real HTML 200 OK pageviews and skips /api/* and error responses.

Instead of manually updating hundreds of database rows after batch-converting legacy PNG/JPG assets to WebP with cwebp -q 82, you can transparently upgrade your Eloquent model accessor:.

You can test your own server's TTFB, HTTP compression headers, and DNS health using our free engineering tools:.

Why deep discounts on used Apple AirPods just aren't worth it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AirPods are expensive, but there are better ways to get them cheaper than the used market.
  • According to recent reports, ever since Apple removed the classic 3.5mm headphone jack, AirPods have taken center stage.
  • The latest AirPods, the AirPods 5, start at around $129.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AirPods are expensive, but there are better ways to get them cheaper than the used market.

According to recent reports, ever since Apple removed the classic 3.5mm headphone jack, AirPods have taken center stage. While you can expect your AirPods to last a good while, nothing lasts forever. You'll eventually need upcoming AirPods if you want to stick with the wireless zeitgeist. Still, it's better to think twice before buying used AirPods to save a quick buck.

The latest AirPods, the AirPods 5, start at around $129. Other than switching to wired headphones or more affordable AirPod alternatives, you may have to wait for a price drop to grab a pair on a budget. And while second-hand tech is a great way to get expensive stuff on the cheap, this doesn't necessarily apply to AirPods.

The biggest concern with used AirPods is hygiene. AirPods that have spent their last life stuck in someone else's ears will be rife with earwax and other skin oils if they haven't been given a proper clean. Apple Support publishes guidelines on how to clean AirPods with methods for each model, so it is possible to pick up a used pair that's completely hygienic. But this doesn't mean any old seller will have done their due diligence, and it's not obvious whether a used pair has been rigorously cleaned or if it's just had its obvious gunk removed.

Recent findings suggest that second-hand AirPods also use standard lithium-ion batteries, which lose capacity over time as each charge cycle ages them. Where this becomes a special risk is that, unlike iPhones, there's no way to know how long your AirPod battery will last. This makes it easy for scammers to charge you too much for a pair near death's door.

In a recent development, these issues and others, such as the plethora of fakes on the market, make buying used AirPods a gamble. Another problem with buying used is that there are many ways to save on AirPods without going pre-owned. While used pairs can be deeply discounted, there's only a small gap in savings between taking that plunge and buying smart.

There are still a lot of upcoming and sealed AirPods on the market. The recently discontinued (but still supported) AirPods 4 can be found for a reasonable price on sites like eBay and Amazon, still in their unopened packaging, which is a safer way to save.

Welcome EmbeddingGemma, Google's latest efficient embedding model

📅 04 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, Google releases EmbeddingGemma, a state-of-the-art multilingual embedding model perfect for on-device use cases.
  • Text embeddings have become the backbone of modern natural‑language applications, turning words, sentences, and documents into dense vectors that capture meaning, sentiment, and intent.
  • It has been revealed that building on this foundation, Google DeepMind’s EmbeddingGemma arrives as the newest, most capable small multilingual embedding model yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Google releases EmbeddingGemma, a state-of-the-art multilingual embedding model perfect for on-device use cases. Designed for speed and efficiency, the model features a compact size of 308M parameters and a 2K context window, unlocking newly introduced possibilities for mobile RAG pipelines, agents, and more. EmbeddingGemma is trained to support over 100 languages and is the highest-ranking text-only multilingual embedding model under 500M on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) at the time of writing.

Text embeddings have become the backbone of modern natural‑language applications, turning words, sentences, and documents into dense vectors that capture meaning, sentiment, and intent. These vectors enable fast similarity search, clustering, classification, and retrieval across massive corpora, powering everything from recommendation engines and semantic search to retrieval-augmented generation and code‑search tools. Embedding models that calculate these embeddings are widely used, with well over 200 million monthly downloads on Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that building on this foundation, Google DeepMind’s EmbeddingGemma arrives as the newest, most capable small multilingual embedding model yet. With just 308M parameters, a 2k‑token context window, and support for over 100 languages, EmbeddingGemma delivers state‑of‑the‑art performance on the Massive Multilingual Text Embedding Benchmark (MMTEB) while staying under 200 MB of RAM when quantized.

The various design choices result in a very practical, open-source tool for computing high-quality multilingual embeddings on everyday devices.

In this blogpost, we describe the EmbeddingGemma architecture and training, and show you how to use the model with various frameworks like Sentence Transformers, LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, txtai, Transformers.js, Text Embedding Inference, and ONNX.

Afterwards, we demonstrate how to finetune EmbeddingGemma on your domain for even stronger performance. In our example, we finetune EmbeddingGemma on the Medical Instruction and Retrieval Dataset (MIRIAD). The resulting model, sentence-transformers/embeddinggemma-300m-medical, achieves state-of-the-art performance on our task: retrieving passages of scientific medical papers in response to detailed medical questions. It even outperforms models twice as massive on this task.

In a recent development, embeddingGemma builds on the Gemma3 transformers backbone, but modified to use bi-directional attention instead of causal (one-way) attention. This means that earlier tokens in the sequence can attend to later tokens, effectively turning the architecture from a decoder into an encoder. Encoder models can outperform LLMs, which are decoders, on embedding tasks like retrieval (Weller et al., 2025). With this backbone, the model can process a sizable 2048 tokens at once, sufficient for typical retrieval inputs, especially given that larger inputs often result in information loss in the text embeddings.

Beyond the fresh Gemma3-based encoder backbone, which produces token embeddings, a mean pooling layer converts these token embeddings into text embeddings. Lastly, two dense layers transform the text embeddings into their final form, a 768-dimensional vector.

The EmbeddingGemma model has been trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), allowing you to truncate the 768‑dimensional output to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions on demand. This results in faster downstream processing and lower memory and disk space utilization. See the Sentence Transformers usage for a snippet showing how to perform this truncation.

It has been revealed that the model has been trained using a carefully curated, multilingual corpus totalling approximately 320 billion tokens. The proprietary dataset is a blend of publicly available web text, code and technical documentation, and synthetic task‑specific examples. It has been filtered to avoid Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM), sensitive data, and low-quality or unsafe content.

Sources indicate that embeddingGemma was benchmarked on the MMTEB (Multilingual, v2) and MTEB (English, v2) suites, which span a wide range of tasks, domains, and languages. Despite its modest 308M‑parameter size, the model consistently beats comparable baselines while keeping a very small memory footprint.

The results will be listed on the official MTEB Leaderboard. We exclude any model that has been trained on more than 20% of the MTEB data, to mitigate potential over‑fitting.

The demo can also be experienced in full screen.

Experience the demo yourself on a Desktop device.

The model has been integrated in Sentence Transformers, and thus also in projects that use Sentence Transformers behind the scenes, such as LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and txtai. See the examples below to get started with your preferred framework.

For production deployments, you can use Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) to serve the model efficiently on various hardware configurations, and you can use Transformers.js for use in web applications.

For embedding models, prompts are prepended to the input text to allow the model to distinguish between different tasks. Because google/embeddinggemma-300m was trained with MRL, the embeddings generated by this model can be truncated to lower dimensionalities without considerably hurting the evaluation performance. Embeddings with lower dimensionalities are both cheaper to store on disk and in memory, as well as faster for downstream tasks like retrieval, clustering, or classification.

In Sentence Transformers, you can set a lower dimensionality using the truncate_dim parameter on either the SentenceTransformer initialization or when calling model.encode/model.encode_query/model.encode_document:.

You can easily deploy EmbeddingGemma for both development and production using Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) version 1.8.1 or later.

Industry observers note that if you run the Docker container with the cuda-1.8.1 tag, it includes support for multiple GPU architectures: Turing, Ampere, Ada Lovelace, and Hopper. For a lighter image tailored to just your GPU, you can instead use a specific tag such as turing-1.8.1, 1.8.1 and 86-1.8.1 (Ampere), 89-1.8.1 (Ada Lovelace), or hopper-1.8.1.

Once deployed, regardless of the device or runtime, you can leverage the /v1/embeddings endpoint based on the OpenAI Embeddings API Specification to generate embeddings.

Alternatively, you can also leverage the /embed endpoint from the Text Embeddings Inference Embeddings API, which supports the prompt_name parameter, meaning there’s no need to manually prepend the prompt to the inputs but select it via prompt_name instead.

Additionally, note that since google/embeddinggemma-300m was trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), you can also leverage the dimensions parameter, on both /v1/embeddings and /embed, to truncate the embeddings to lower dimensionalities (512, 256, and 128) without hurting the evaluation performance.

In a recent development, you can also run the model directly with ONNX Runtime, making it highly portable and cross-platform compatible. The example below demonstrates usage in Python, but the same approach can be applied in other languages (Java, C#, C++, etc.) as well.

As with all models compatible with the Sentence Transformers library, EmbeddingGemma can be easily fine-tuned on your specific dataset. To showcase this, we'll be finetuning google/embeddinggemma-300m on the Medical Instruction and RetrIeval Dataset (MIRIAD) dataset, such that our finetuned model becomes particularly adept at finding passages up to 1000 tokens from scientific medical papers given detailed medical questions. These passages can be used as crucial context for a generative model to answer questions more effectively.

In a recent development, below, you can explore each key component of the finetuning process using expandable tabs. Each tab contains the relevant code and a detailed explanation.

According to recent reports, this code loads the EmbeddingGemma model from Hugging Face, with optional model card metadata for documentation and sharing. The SentenceTransformer class loads the model weights and configuration, while the model_card_data argument attaches metadata useful for inclusion in the automatically generated model card.

This code loads the MIRIAD dataset, or rather, a copy that has been divided into train, eval, and test splits. Using a large, high-quality dataset ensures the model learns meaningful representations, while subsetting allows for faster experimentation. The load_dataset function fetches the dataset from Hugging Face Datasets, and the .select() method limits the number of samples for each split.

This code defines the loss function for training, using Cached Multiple Negatives Ranking Loss (CMNRL). CMNRL is effective for retrieval tasks, as it uses in-batch negatives to efficiently train the model to distinguish between correct and incorrect pairs. The loss takes question-answer pairs and treats other answers in the batch as negatives, maximizing the distance between unrelated pairs in the embedding space. The mini_batch_size parameter controls the memory usage, but does not affect the training dynamics.

In a recent development, it's recommended to use this loss with a large per_device_train_batch_size in SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments and a low mini_batch_size in CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss for a strong training signal with low memory usage. Additionally, the NO_DUPLICATES batch sampler is recommended to avoid accidental false negatives.

Recent findings suggest that this code sets up all hyperparameters and configuration for training, evaluation, and logging. Proper training arguments are crucial for efficient, stable, and reproducible training. The arguments control batch sizes, learning rate, mixed precision, evaluation and saving frequency, and more. Notably, the prompts dictionary maps dataset columns to prompts used by the model to distinguish queries from documents.

This code sets up an evaluator for information retrieval, using queries and a corpus to measure model performance. Evaluation during training helps monitor progress and avoid overfitting. The evaluator computes retrieval metrics (NDCG, MRR, Recall, Precision, MAP, etc.) by checking if the model retrieves the correct passages for each query. It can be run before, during, and after training, and the results will be logged and incorporated in the automatically generated model card.

Note that this snippet in particular uses all (1k) evaluation questions against a corpus of all (1k) evaluation passages and 30k training passages, for a total of 31k documents. Evaluating only against evaluation passages is too simple for the model.

This code initializes and runs the training loop, coordinating all components.

If desired, you can further reduce the memory footprint by reducing mini_batch_size on the CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss and batch_size on the InformationRetrievalEvaluator instances. The performance of the base model was already excellent, with a strong 0.8340 NDCG@10 on our MIRIAD test set. Despite that, we were able to increase it considerably on this domain-specific dataset.

Our fine-tuning process achieved a significant improvement of +0.0522 NDCG@10 on the test set, resulting in a model that comfortably outperforms any existing general-purpose embedding model on our specific task, at this model size. Additional time and compute investment would allow for even stronger results, such as hard negatives mining or training with more than 100k data pairs.

Welcome EmbeddingGemma! This is an exciting step forward for developers who need powerful multilingual embeddings without the heavy resource requirements of larger models. A 308M-parameter model that supports more than 100 languages while achieving top-tier performance on MTEB is impressive..... especially for teams building applications..... that need to run efficiently on mobile devices and edge hardware. The combination of speed, compact size, and a 2K context window makes it a practical solution for real-world retrieval and semantic search tasks.

What stands out most is the potential impact on on-device AI..... experiences. As more applications move toward privacy-focused and low-latency processing, efficient embedding models like EmbeddingGemma can help make advanced RAG systems, AI agents, and multilingual search.... features accessible to a much wider audience. It's great to see Google investing in models.... that balance performance with efficiency, opening the door for innovative use.... cases across smartphones, embedded systems, and resource-constrained environments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Designers hand you a brand hex like #3B82F6-ish, and your Tailwind config has 11 shades per color. Which one is "closest"? Eyeballing it leads to inconsistent UIs.

Sources indicate that euclidean distance in RGB treats all channels equally, but human vision doesn't. Two colors can be numerically close and look different (especially in greens). A better approach is to compare in a perceptual space such as CIELAB (deltaE).

Industry observers note that nearest shade is only half the story. Check the text/background pair against WCAG 4.5:1 for body text. A shade that matches the brand but fails contrast needs a darker neighbor for text.

I built a free, client-side tool that does the matching in your browser (nothing uploaded): Colors to Tailwind. Pair it with the contrast checker to validate accessibility.

#80931. Tech Report: A tempo slider that's off by default: half time, double time and a 90 BPM starting point

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (510 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A tempo slider that's off by default: half time, double time and a 90 BPM starting point

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I build FightNome, so this post is about my own app.
  • FightNome is a pad-work trainer for boxing, Muay Thai, kickboxing and MMA.
  • The settings screen says so in one line, calling 90 BPM a pace built for clean technique.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I build FightNome, so this post is about my own app.

FightNome is a pad-work trainer for boxing, Muay Thai, kickboxing and MMA. A recorded human voice calls strikes on the beat of a backing track, and you throw them on a bag, on pads or in the air while the phone sits in your pocket. Because everything happens on a beat, tempo is the main thing that decides how hard a round feels. You'd expect a substantial tempo slider on the first screen. There isn't one.

Workouts run at 90 BPM by default. The settings screen says so in one line, calling 90 BPM a pace built for clean technique. If you want to change it for a whole workout, you turn on "Tempo control" in Settings and a workout-wide slider appears. The range it can cover is 74 to 128 BPM.

Industry observers note that for everyday changes there's a smaller control on each section of a workout. It has three steps:.

So the common case, "this round should feel faster", is handled per section with three choices, and the precise BPM number lives one setting away.

It has been revealed that A slider with a number on it invites a specific mistake. People who train alone tend to push the pace because faster feels like harder work. On a beat that means calls arrive before the last strike is back in guard, and the round turns into slapping at the bag to keep up. A default that's described as "built for clean technique" sets the expectation before anyone touches anything.

According to recent reports, the other reason is that BPM is a music number, not a training number. "128" means nothing to someone who wants to hit pads. "Double time" does, and so does "half time" on a heavy round where you want to sit down on every shot.

It has been revealed that section-level intensity also fits how a real session is put together. A workout in the app is made of sections, either striking or conditioning (rope, shadow, bodyweight), each with rounds and rest. One slow technical section and one fast one in the same workout is a normal plan, and a single global slider can't express it.

Two more controls live inside the combo editor, on single tiles:.

In a recent development, these came from the same thinking. Most of what makes a combo feel right is where the gaps are, and that's easier to shape one tile at a time than with one number for the whole session.

According to recent reports, I'm still unsure about the name "Tempo control" for the setting that reveals the slider. If you've hidden an advanced control behind a toggle, what did you call it so people could find it?

Recent findings suggest that fightNome is on the App Store (iOS 26 and up) and Google Play. It's a paid subscription, see the store for the current price. More at https://fightnome.app.

I used AI assistance to draft this note and edited it myself.

#80928. robots.txt can't block AI crawlers, but something can

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (998 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

robots.txt can't block AI crawlers, but something can

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, your robots.txt file does not block anyone.
  • Your site is now read by AI crawlers that collect training data, search bots that decide whether you appear in chatbot answers, and fetchers that pull your pages when a user asks a question.
  • Industry observers note that RFC 9309 formalized the Robots Exclusion Protocol in 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, your robots.txt file does not block anyone. It is a text file full of polite requests, and the standard behind it notes so in plain words. RFC 9309, the IETF specification for the Robots Exclusion Protocol, states that the rules "are not a form of access authorization.".

That matters more than it used to. Your site is now read by AI crawlers that collect training data, search bots that decide whether you appear in chatbot answers, and fetchers that pull your pages when a user asks a question. If you want a say in any of that, it helps to know what robots.txt actually does, who is listening, and what to add when a request is not enough.

Industry observers note that RFC 9309 formalized the Robots Exclusion Protocol in 2022. The spec says crawlers are requested to honor the rules in your file. Requested. Nothing puts the file between a crawler and your server: a cooperative crawler fetches robots.txt separately and decides for itself whether to comply, and nothing in the protocol can stop a request. Well-behaved crawlers comply because their operators choose to comply. Cloudflare's documentation puts it directly: robots.txt directives are voluntary, and crawlers can ignore them.

According to recent reports, openAI documents three user agents. GPTBot crawls content that may be used to train its foundation models, and disallowing GPTBot tells OpenAI your content should not be used for that training. OAI-SearchBot is used to surface websites in ChatGPT search results; OpenAI says sites that opt out of it will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers, though they can still appear as navigational links. ChatGPT-User fetches a page when a user asks ChatGPT something; because these requests are user-initiated, OpenAI notes that robots.txt rules may not apply. The settings are independent, and OpenAI says search can take about 24 hours to adjust to a robots.txt update.

Industry observers note that anthropic documents a similar split. ClaudeBot collects web content that could contribute to model training, Claude-SearchBot works on search result quality, and Claude-User handles fetches directed by a user's question. Anthropic claims its bots honor robots.txt directives, supports the non-standard Crawl-delay extension, and asks you to set the rules on every subdomain you want covered. As of October 30, 2026, Anthropic has also begun recognizing a machine-readable signal, based on IETF draft work, that lets a site express a "no AI training" preference, with the rollout happening over time. A robots.txt rule that names ClaudeBot directly takes priority over that general signal.

Recent findings suggest that the practical consequence: "allow AI" and "block AI" are not your only options. You can disallow the training crawlers while allowing the search crawlers, so your pages can still be cited in chatbot answers. That split is the part most site owners miss.

If you want certainty instead of cooperation, the block has to happen on the request path itself: a CDN or WAF rule, your origin server, or your app requiring a login. Cloudflare's AI Crawler and Agent access policies are the clearest example. You set an action for each behavior (Search, Agent, Training), and the Block action stops matching requests at Cloudflare's edge. Two details are worth knowing. The Training behavior also offers a Disallow action that only writes robots.txt directives, which stay voluntary unless you enable the option that additionally blocks AI training crawlers at the edge. And for newly introduced domains, all three behaviors default to Allow, so doing nothing is itself a choice.

In a recent development, you can do the same thing without Cloudflare: deny requests by user agent in your server configuration, or block the published IP ranges the labs maintain (OpenAI publishes a JSON list per bot). One caveat from Anthropic's documentation: blocking their crawler IPs can impede their ability to read your robots.txt, so they warn it may not work as a persistent opt-out on its own. My advice: keep robots.txt as the stated preference, and treat request-path rules as the enforcement layer, not a replacement for the file.

Blocking is only half of the decision. The llms.txt proposal, first published in 2024 and updated to v2 in 2026, suggests a markdown file on your site that gives agents concise, expert-level information plus links to markdown versions of your pages. It is a proposal, not a standard, but it notes that thousands of sites now publish one, and OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini publish their own. If you want AI assistants to describe your product accurately, this is the constructive counterpart to robots.txt: one file states what stays out, the other helps what comes in get read correctly.

This part is advice, not documentation. Ask three questions. Do I want my content in training datasets? Do I want it in AI search answers? Do I want user-triggered fetches to work? Then write one robots.txt group per bot to match your answers. If "no" needs to mean "no," put a real block behind it, whether that is a CDN rule, a server rule or a login wall. If you want to be read well, consider an llms.txt. None of it is permanent; you can change the file tomorrow.

robots.txt is where you state your preference, and the standard itself says it is not access authorization. The major AI labs document separate bots for training, search and user-triggered fetches, so you can choose per purpose. Only a control on the request path, a CDN rule, your server configuration or a login, can actually stop a request. And llms.txt exists for the opposite goal: helping agents read what you want them to read.

The next step is small. Open your robots.txt, decide what it should say about each bot, and decide whether your "no" needs enforcement behind it.

Source pages: RFC 9309: Robots Exclusion Protocol, OpenAI crawlers, Anthropic's crawler documentation, Cloudflare AI Crawler and Agent access policies, The llms.txt proposal.

#80927. Tech Report: mmBERT: ModernBERT goes Multilingual

📅 09 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1341 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: mmBERT: ModernBERT goes Multilingual

📅 09 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1341 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this blog post introduces mmBERT, a state-of-the-art massively multilingual encoder model trained on 3T+ tokens of text in over 1800 languages.
  • If you are interested in trying out the models yourself, some example boilerplate is available at the end of this blogpost!
  • mmBERT was trained on a carefully curated multilingual dataset totaling over 3T tokens across three distinct training phases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this blog post introduces mmBERT, a state-of-the-art massively multilingual encoder model trained on 3T+ tokens of text in over 1800 languages. It shows significant performance and speed improvements over previous multilingual models, being the first to improve upon XLM-R, while also developing new strategies for effectively learning low-resource languages. mmBERT builds upon ModernBERT for a blazingly fast architecture, and adds novel components to enable efficient multilingual learning.

If you are interested in trying out the models yourself, some example boilerplate is available at the end of this blogpost!

mmBERT was trained on a carefully curated multilingual dataset totaling over 3T tokens across three distinct training phases. The foundation of our training data consists of three primary open-source and high-quality web crawls that enable both multilingual coverage and data quality:.

DCLM and Filtered DCLM provides the highest quality English content available, serving as the backbone for strong English performance (with the filtered data coming from Dolmino). This dataset represents state-of-the-art web filtering techniques and forms a crucial component. Due to the high quality of this data, we use a signficantly higher proportion of English than previous generation multilingual encoder models (up to 18%).

It has been revealed that fineWeb2 delivers broad multilingual web content covering over 1,800 languages. This dataset enables our extensive multilingual coverage while maintaining reasonable quality standards across diverse language families and scripts.

It has been revealed that fineWeb2-HQ consists of a filtered subset of FineWeb2 focusing on 20 high-resource languages. This filtered version provides higher-quality multilingual content that bridges the gap between English-only filtered data and broad multilingual coverage.

The training data also incorporates specialized corpora from Dolma, MegaWika v2, ProLong and more: code repositories (StarCoder, ProLong), academic content (ArXiv, PeS2o), reference materials (Wikipedia, textbooks), and community discussions (StackExchange), along with instruction and mathematical datasets.

The key innovation in our data approach is the progressive language inclusion strategy shown in Figure 1. At each phase we progressively sample from a flatter distribution (i.e. closer to uniform), while also adding new languages. This means that high resource languages like Russian start off with a high percentage of the data (i.e. 9%) and then in the last phase of training end around half of that. We start with 60 high-resource languages during pre-training, expand to 110 languages during mid-training, and finally include all 1,833 languages from FineWeb2 during the decay phase. This allows us to maximize the impact of limited low-resource language data without excess reptitions and while maintaining high overall data quality.

mmBERT builds upon the ModernBERT architecture but introduces several key innovations for multilingual learning:.

According to recent reports, we use the same core architecture as ModernBERT-base with 22 layers and 1152 intermediate dimensions, but switch to the Gemma 2 tokenizer to better handle multilingual text. The base model has 110M non-embedding parameters (307M total due to the larger vocabulary), while the small variant has 42M non-embedding parameters (140M total).

Our training follows a carefully designed three-phase schedule:.

Industry observers note that inverse Mask Ratio Schedule: Instead of using a fixed masking rate, we progressively reduce the mask ratio from 30% → 15% → 5% across training phases. This allows the model to learn basic representations with higher masking early on, then focus on more nuanced understanding with lower masking rates.

Annealed Language Learning: We dynamically adjust the temperature for multilingual data sampling from τ=0.7 → 0.5 → 0.3. This creates a progression from high-resource language bias toward more uniform sampling, enabling the model to build a strong multilingual foundation before learning low-resource languages.

In a recent development, progressive Language Addition: Rather than training on all languages simultaneously, we strategically add languages at each phase (60 → 110 → 1,833). This maximizes learning efficiency by avoiding excessive epochs on limited low-resource data while still achieving strong performance.

Model Merging: We train three different variants during the decay phase (English-focused, 110-language, and all-language) and use TIES merging to combine their strengths into the final model.

English Performance: On the English GLUE benchmark (Table 1), mmBERT base achieves strong performance, substantially outperforming other multilingual models like XLM-R (multilingual RoBERTa) base and mGTE base, while remaining competitive to English-only models despite less than 25% of the mmBERT training data being English.

Multilingual Performance: mmBERT shows significant improvements on XTREME benchmark compared to XLM-R as demonstrated in Table 2. Notable gains include strong performance on XNLI classification, substantial improvements in question answering tasks like TyDiQA, and competitive results across PAWS-X and XCOPA for cross-lingual understanding.

The model performs well across most categories, with the exception of some structured prediction tasks like NER and POS tagging, likely due to tokenizer differences that affect word boundary detection. On these categories, it performs about the same as the previous generation, but can be applied to more languages.

English Retrieval: Even though mmBERT is designed for massively multilingual settings, in the MTEB v2 English benchmarks (Table 3), mmBERT highlights significant gains over previous multilingual models and even ties the capabilities of English-only models like ModernBERT!

Multilingual Retrieval: mmBERT shows consistent improvements on MTEB v2 multilingual benchmarks compared to other models (Table 4).

Sources indicate that code Retrieval: Due to the modern tokenizer (based on Gemma 2) mmBERT also highlights strong coding performance (Table 5), making mmBERT suitable for any type of textual data. The only model that outperforms it is EuroBERT, which was able to use the non-publicly accessible Stack v2 dataset.

Sources indicate that one of mmBERT's most significant novel features is demonstrating that low-resource languages can be effectively learned during the short decay phase of training. We validated this approach by testing on languages only introduced during the final 100B token decay phase.

According to recent reports, dramatic Performance Gains: Testing on TiQuaD (Tigrinya) and FoQA (Faroese), we observed substantial improvements when these languages were included in the decay phase, as shown in Figure 2. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our progressive language learning approach.

Recent findings suggest that competitive with Large Models: Despite only seeing these languages in the final training phase, mmBERT achieves performance levels that exceed much larger models. On Faroese question answering where LLMs have been benchmarked, mmBERT outperforms Google Gemini 2.5 Pro and OpenAI o3.

Sources indicate that rapid Learning Mechanism: The success of decay-phase language learning stems from the model's ability to leverage its strong multilingual foundation built during earlier phases. When exposed to new languages, the model can quickly adapt existing cross-lingual representations rather than learning from scratch.

Model Merging Benefits: The final mmBERT models successfully retain most of the decay-phase improvements while benefiting from the English-focused and high-resource variants through TIES merging.

mmBERT delivers substantial efficiency gains over previous multilingual encoder models through architectural improvements inherited from ModernBERT:.

Throughput Performance: mmBERT processes text significantly faster than existing multilingual models across various sequence lengths, as demonstrated in Figure 3. Both the small and base models show substantial speed improvements over previous multilingual encoders.

Modern Architecture Benefits: The efficiency gains come from two main technical improvements:.

Sequence Length Scaling: Unlike older models limited to 512 tokens, mmBERT handles up to 8,192 tokens efficiently while maintaining high throughput. This makes it suitable for longer document processing tasks that are increasingly common in multilingual applications.

Energy Efficiency: The combination of better throughput and modern architecture results in lower computational costs for inference, making mmBERT more practical for production deployments where multilingual support is needed at scale.

These efficiency improvements make mmBERT not just more accurate than previous multilingual encoders, but also significantly more practical for real usage.

You can use these models with just a few lines of code!

I would suggest checking out https://github.com/Tiiiger/bert_score for more details and perhaps raising an problem there if it's unclear.

Dynamo 1.6.2 Turns an Oversized-Prompt HTTP 500 Into a 400: Why Error Codes Decide Your Retry Load, Plus the Opt-In GC Freeze for SGLang Workers

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that NVIDIA Dynamo v1.6.2 (tagged 2026-11-05) is a patch release on v1.6.1, and the two changes worth your attention are small in code and large in operations.
  • According to recent reports, status codes are not cosmetic.
  • Industry observers note that before 1.6.2, an oversized non-streaming /v1/messages request on the TensorRT-LLM backend returned a 500.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that NVIDIA Dynamo v1.6.2 (tagged 2026-11-05) is a patch release on v1.6.1, and the two changes worth your attention are small in code and large in operations. First, a TensorRT-LLM prompt longer than the engine's max_num_tokens now returns HTTP 400 invalid_request_error instead of HTTP 500 api_error, and the worker keeps running. Second, SGLang decode and aggregated workers get an opt-in --freeze-gc-after-init flag (DYN_SGL_FREEZE_GC_AFTER_INIT) meant to reduce streaming stalls in long-running workers. Backend versions are unchanged from v1.6.1: SGLang v0.5.21, TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0rc29, vLLM v0.31.0. Below, the release notes' statements are kept separate from my own arithmetic, and the charts are marked illustrative.

According to recent reports, status codes are not cosmetic. They are the contract that every layer between the user and the GPU uses to decide what to do next.

Industry observers note that before 1.6.2, an oversized non-streaming /v1/messages request on the TensorRT-LLM backend returned a 500. The v1.6.0 release notes list this as a known matter with no workaround. A request that can never succeed was labeled as a transient server failure. Any retry policy that treats 5xx as retryable then re-sends a request that fails identically every time.

Here is the simple arithmetic. Suppose a client library allows 3 retries on 5xx. One oversized prompt becomes 4 attempts that reach the frontend. If 50 requests per second are oversized (a misconfigured agent loop pasting a whole repository into context is a realistic source), that is 200 attempts per second of pure waste, versus 50 with a 400. The numbers in the chart below are illustrative, not measured. The point is the multiplier, which is set by your retry policy and not by Dynamo.

There is a second cost. Error-rate dashboards and SLO burn alerts usually count 5xx as your failures and 4xx as the caller's. An api_error spike from oversized prompts pages the on-call engineer for something that is not an outage. Moving the response to 400 puts the signal in the right bucket.

Industry observers note that the release notes flag one item as able to affect existing workflows: the SGLang image's Python change. Because the image no longer uses Ubuntu's libpython3.12, cuda-gdb inside that image no longer supports Python scripting. If your debugging runbook relies on Python pretty-printers in cuda-gdb, read that line twice.

Recent findings suggest that you can test the contract directly. The sketch below sends a deliberately oversized prompt and reports the status. The endpoint, model name, and sizes are placeholders you set for your own deployment.

It has been revealed that then check the layers in front of it. Three places commonly retry on 5xx without anyone remembering they do:.

Log the attempt count per request id for a day. If oversized prompts show up as repeated attempts, the fix is not only the upgrade. Add a cheap pre-check at the gateway that rejects prompts over the token budget before they reach a GPU worker, and make the budget a shared configuration value rather than a number copied into three repositories.

One more detail from the v1.6.0 known-problems list: when a worker rejects a request, the frontend returns a generic error without the worker's message. The 1.6.2 notes carry the v1.6.0 known issues forward except the oversized-prompt one, so on 1.6.2 you should expect the correct class of status but not necessarily a helpful body. Do not build client logic that parses error text.

It has been revealed that the second change targets Python's garbage collector inside SGLang decode and aggregated workers. The release notes describe the goal as reducing streaming stalls in long-running workers, state that it is off by default, and advise checking memory use against a control worker before enabling it widely.

The mechanism it builds on is standard CPython. The cyclic collector periodically walks tracked container objects looking for reference cycles. In a worker that loaded a large amount of Python state at startup (config objects, tokenizer structures, scheduler tables), each full collection has a lot to walk, and a long walk is a pause on a thread that may also be feeding tokens to streams. Python exposes gc.freeze(), which moves everything at the moment tracked into a permanent generation that later collections skip. The release notes name the flag; I have not read the implementation, so treat the following as the general technique and not a description of Dynamo's code.

It has been revealed that run it on your own hardware. Exact numbers depend on the machine and object count, but the shape is consistent: the pause drops once long-lived startup objects stop being scanned. The trade-off is built in as well. Frozen objects are never collected, so any cycle among them that later becomes garbage stays in memory. That is why the advice to compare against a control worker is the right one.

If you have no inter-token gap metric today, add one first. Without it you cannot tell whether the flag helped.

Recent findings suggest that the compatibility table is unchanged from v1.6.1, which is itself useful: a patch that does not move the engine versions means model-level behavior should not shift. What can shift is the runtime underneath.

According to recent reports, note how far these pins sit from the newest upstream tags. As of 2026-11-21, vLLM's latest tag is v0.34.0 and SGLang's is v0.5.23, so a Dynamo image is a tested bundle that trails the engines' newest releases by design. If you need a specific engine feature, check the pin before you assume the image has it.

For the upgrade diff, look at three things in this order: the image's Python version and any native wheels you layer on top (the SGLang change replaces the interpreter), the Mooncake floor if you use KV transfer, and any debugging tooling that touches cuda-gdb Python scripting.

Does 1.6.2 fix every oversized-prompt path? The notes say it fixes the v1.6.0 known issue for non-streaming /v1/messages on TensorRT-LLM. They claim nothing about other backends, so test each backend you run.

According to recent reports, will clients now stop retrying? Only if their policy treats 400 as non-retryable, which is the common default. Verify yours with a probe like the one above.

Is --freeze-gc-after-init safe to turn on everywhere? The notes ship it off by default and recommend comparing memory against a control worker first. Treat it as a canary-first change.

Does the patch change model outputs? Engine pins are unchanged from v1.6.1, so the release does not move engine versions. Rebuilt images still deserve your normal regression run.

Recent findings suggest that where is the primary source? The v1.6.2 release notes on the project's GitHub releases page, and the v1.6.0 notes for the known-issues list this patch partly resolves.

Sources: NVIDIA Dynamo v1.6.2 and v1.6.0 release notes (github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/releases); vLLM and SGLang release tags on GitHub, checked 2026-11-21.

Merge #2: my five pre-upload tools are now one suite

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (416 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last month I audited my own fleet — 44 published open-source tools — and the audit ordered 18 of the quiet ones merged into 4 flagships.
  • According to recent reports, faceless-qc-lite started in October as a free pre-upload checker for faceless videos: loudness, dead air, black frames, caption speed, resolution — five checks on the video file, one PASS/HOLD receipt.
  • pipx install faceless-qc-lite faceless-qc-lite suite my-video.mp4 --captions my-video.srt --thumbnail thumb.png --title "My Title" --hashtags "#shorts" --catalogue catalogue.json.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last month I audited my own fleet — 44 published open-source tools — and the audit ordered 18 of the quiet ones merged into 4 flagships. Merge #1 turned five AI-agent-setup auditors into preflight-agent. Merge #2, shipping now, is the creator side: faceless-qc-lite v2.0.0.

According to recent reports, faceless-qc-lite started in October as a free pre-upload checker for faceless videos: loudness, dead air, black frames, caption speed, resolution — five checks on the video file, one PASS/HOLD receipt. It did that job well. It also sat next to five other tools I'd built for the rest of the same upload: caption-toolkit, thumbnail-checker, retention-checker, shorts-packager, link-rot. Six installs to answer one question: is this upload ready? Now it's one:.

pipx install faceless-qc-lite faceless-qc-lite suite my-video.mp4 --captions my-video.srt --thumbnail thumb.png --title "My Title" --hashtags "#shorts" --catalogue catalogue.json.

It has been revealed that one run, one receipt. A module with nothing to run on reports SKIPPED, with its reason — a skip is never counted as a pass. Suite verdict: HOLD if anything HOLDs or FAILs (exit 2), PASS WITH WARNINGS if anything warns (exit 0), else PASS.

The merge changed no engine: every engine is byte-identical to its source, verdict vocabularies stay per-module, 21 fresh tests on top of 220 carried over — 241 total, all green.

The fixture is the demo: examples/make_fixture.py builds a set with one planted problem per module: a very quiet 640x360 video with a 3.5s black gap, a caption cue racing at 138 CPS, a 320x180 thumbnail, a 103-character title, a catalogue with a goo.gl link and an example.com placeholder. The README reproduces the real suite receipt verbatim — HOLD, all six sections, exit 2.

It has been revealed that watch it run (17 seconds): the short demo video is a real pre-upload run of the original checker — an upload-ready faceless video measured at −21.6 LUFS against the −14 target and held. That catch is why this tool exists. Watch the demo.

Recent findings suggest that honest limits: ffmpeg is a hard requirement for the media measurements. The link audit is structural — it has never loaded your link. A PASS means "none of the checked problems were found" — not "this video will perform". It's MIT, zero dependencies (stdlib only), local only, no telemetry, and the anchor stays free forever.

Repo: https://github.com/jasveerai88/faceless-qc-lite.

Feedback I'd most value: uploads the suite misjudges — a failure mode none of the six checks sees, or a verdict the measurements don't support.

#80919. Latest Update: Jupyter Agents: training LLMs to reason with notebooks

📅 10 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2127 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Jupyter Agents: training LLMs to reason with notebooks

📅 10 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the past year has been all about giving LLMs more tools and autonomy to solve more complex and open ended tasks.
  • A natural way to display multi-step code execution together with reasoning is within a Jupyter Notebook, which consists of code and markdown cells.
  • While large models are starting to show useful behavior, the key question is how we can continue improving them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the past year has been all about giving LLMs more tools and autonomy to solve more complex and open ended tasks. The goal of the Jupyter Agent is to give the model the ultimate tool: code execution.

A natural way to display multi-step code execution together with reasoning is within a Jupyter Notebook, which consists of code and markdown cells. So we built Jupyter Agent to act as an agent that can execute code directly inside a Jupyter notebook and use this environment to solve data analysis and data science tasks. Think of it like Cursor, but living natively inside your data science workflow.We built a demo of this vision with Qwen-3 Coder, at the moment one of the strongest coding models. This is a follow-up to our earlier work on jupyter-agent (v1).

While large models are starting to show useful behavior, the key question is how we can continue improving them. To this end, we focus on strengthening smaller models to perform well on agentic data science tasks as they at the moment struggle to compete with the large models.

The goal of this project is to build a pipeline to first generate high-quality training data, then fine-tune an existing small model, and finally evaluate whether the model's performance improves on relevant benchmarks.

Let’s begin with the last step: selecting a strong benchmark for evaluating models on data science tasks.

In order to understand if we are making progress towards better data science agents we need a benchmark to measure such capabilities. Last year, in partnership with Adyen, we introduced the DABStep benchmark: a way to evaluate data science agents on realistic tasks. The setup is simple: provide the LLM with datasets and ask it to answer non-trivial data questions.

Sources indicate that this benchmark remains challenging for today’s LLMs — e.g. the best out-of-the-box model is Claude 4 Sonnet which reaches not even 20% accuracy on the hard tasks.You can explore the live leaderboard here.

Now that we identified a good benchmark we can try to climb it! We set out to build a dataset for fine-tuning such that even a small data agent model could perform well on DABStep.

Our first choice was Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507: extremely small (fast to iterate with, easy to run), yet strong enough to act in agentic scenarios.

Sources indicate that not great — but a promising starting point, since it left a lot of room for improvement. Let's see how we can improve it!

Industry observers note that A core aspect of agents that sets it apart from a pure chat model is the scaffolding built around the model to steer its behaviour. The evaluation script in DABStep for example uses smolagents to execute code. Smolagents comes with predefined behaviors, prompting structures, and expected formats.

We also studied the Qwen-Agent codebase, where the authors tailoring scaffolding to the model. This makes sense: Claude Code, for example, works shockingly well with Claude Sonnet because their scaffolding is aligned.

So, we restructured our scaffolding:.

Results: accuracy jumped from 44.4% → 59.7% (easy split). 🚀.

With simplified scaffolding in place, we focused on fine-tuning Qwen3-4B for data science agentic tasks.

Industry observers note that the recipe to improve a model on a certain task or behaviour is to train it on data that reflects the tasks as closely as possible. A natural starting point is to look at real Jupyter Notebooks and find notebooks that align closely with the task that we blueprint to tackle, namely data analysis.

Kaggle notebooks offer a wealth of high quality data analysis notebooks and are made available by Kaggle:.

It has been revealed that now that we have good results with a base model it's time to build a dataset that will help us improve it even further. We designed a multi-stage pipeline using Datatrove to clean and prepare Kaggle notebooks at scale.

In a recent development, we started with ~2TB of Kaggle notebooks and reduced it to ~250GB reusing our work from the BigCode project. As part of the StarCoder2 training data processing the notebooks (without output cells) were already deduplicated. Most Kaggle notebooks are small variations or near-identical copies, so this step was essential.Key insight: ~90% of raw notebooks are duplicates, which would have skewed training if left unfiltered.

Most Kaggle notebooks reference external datasets via Kaggle metadata. To make sure the code inside notebooks could actually run, we built a pipeline that automatically fetched these linked datasets. This step was crucial, since many notebooks would otherwise be incomplete or non-executable.

Using the kagglehub package, we downloaded thousands of datasets — about 5TB in total. To keep things manageable and relevant:.

By the end, we had a rich collection of executable notebooks paired with their datasets, providing the foundation for training agents in realistic, runnable environments.

We scored notebooks based on educational quality using Qwen3-32B. We saw that using the whole notebook was not optimal, as many contained trivial or broken code. Our educational scoring approach is detailed in edu_scoring.py.

TL;DR: We assigned each notebook a score from 1–5 based on clarity, completeness, and educational value, and kept only those above a chosen threshold. This filtering removed about 70% of the notebooks.

Sources indicate that this is similar to the insight from the BeyondWeb paper, which demonstrated that using high-quality data is better for synthetic data generation — a step we relied on for QA (Question-Answer) generation. This helped the model learn from “high quality” notebooks instead of noisy ones.

We excluded notebooks about training LLMs or unrelated to data analysis. We also removed notebooks that didn’t actually use datasets through an automated LLM-based filtering process using Qwen3-32B. The implementation of filtering can be found in extract_packages_and_files.py.

It has been revealed that TL;DR: We prompted Qwen3-32B to identify and remove notebooks that either (1) had nothing to do with data analysis, or (2) didn’t actually use datasets. This step removed about 20% of the notebooks.

This ensured we trained only on relevant data science tasks.

Using the cleaned notebooks, we generated question–answer pairs using Qwen3-32B. The questions and answer are grounded in the real notebook traces so the QA pairs are based on real code execution results. Prompt design: we asked the LLM to produce natural questions that could realistically be asked of the dataset, then validated whether the notebook provided a correct answer.

Challenge: We had to try many prompts to get higher-difficulty questions because LLMs tended to generate trivial ones like "what is the size of the dataset".Insight: We broke this into two steps because LLMs tended to hallucinate answers:.

The complete prompting strategy and implementation is available in generate_qa.py.

Recent findings suggest that finally we want to generate clean code execution traces since even the original notebooks after processing are often open ended and verbose with lots of irrelevant parts. However, we want our Jupyter Agent to get to the result efficiently. To generate cleaner notebook traces for training we generated traces synthetically based on the original notebooks.We have prompted Qwen-3-Coder-480B model to generate a jupyter notebook code to answer the question from the previously generated synthetic QA pair. Traces captured step-by-step code execution, including intermediate outputs, which are crucial for agent training.

We used E2B for our agent to solve the synthetic QA pairs, which required fetching Kaggle datasets so the code could actually run via E2B.

Challenge 1: Many datasets were unavailable.Trick: Since LLMs are strong at code and have a decent world model, we prompted them to act as a code interpreter when the dataset was missing.

Sources indicate that challenge 2: Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B model does not support thinking mode - how can we extract code commentary? By default it often outputs just a brief comment followed by several steps of code execution. However, we'd like some reasoning or comments between every cell. Trick: When switching from Qwen3-32B to Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B we noticed that often output message content was empty. This turns out to be a previously known quirk of Qwen3-Coder models in which when using tool calling the model would not return an empty assistant response. We enforce some text commentary through tooling by passing 'comment' as a required field in the code execution tool call. This way when non-reasoning model is used for code cell generation it will by default output some description of its actions from 1st POV, emulating the thinking traces structure.

Note: the generated final answer in the notebook may vary from the answer specified in the QA pair. This is caused by the fact that the agent model could use data preprocessing methods and steps different from the original Kaggle notebook and the synthetic question would not usually specify them. This discrepancy is normal and lays the foundation for a fresh exciting research direction of how language models tend to treat data analysis and whether they do it differently from humans. For full transparency we keep both LLM-generated final answer and original answer from the real Kaggle notebook as a signal of model's performance. We encourage the community to try different dataset mixes to see how they can push performance even further.

We truncated overly long outputs and filtered out trivial traces to prevent content length issues and keep only high-quality traces.We kept non-trivial, multi-turn traces aligned with DABStep-style tasks.The resulting Jupyter Agent Dataset became the foundation for SFT on Qwen3-4B models with 51k synthetic notebooks and almost 0.2B tokens.

With this dataset in hand, the natural next step is to see whether it actually helps our model become a stronger data science agent. Let’s move on to the training pipeline and evaluate the impact!

Sources indicate that with the curated dataset ready, we turned to the key question: does this data actually help the model get better at solving data analysis tasks? To find out, we set up a simple fine-tuning pipeline and ran experiments to measure the impact of training on our synthetic notebooks.

Some training steps turned out to be particularly interesting and gave us useful insights:.

Our complete training implementation, including hyperparameter configurations and template adaptations, is available in our finetuning directory in our repo.

Recent findings suggest that first, we generated our final dataset using Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B which contains high quality code and short reasoning-like traces. Afterwards, we started our training and we have experimented with various configurations like PEFT/adapters vs. full-parameter tuning, learning rate, number of epochs, adding noise and others. We found out, that full-parameter fine-tuning allows the model to learn and replicate the Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B behavior response quality better with shorter supporting commentary fitting more to the data analysis task without unnecessary long reasoning.

Industry observers note that we have done a small ablation study on the impact of no. training epochs:.

We observe that it is beneficial to have a bit more epochs than usual for SFT with lower learning rate and higher neftune noise (7). Finally, we compare our trained models with implemented scaffolding to define the pure impact of our training dataset. In summary, we can see up to 36%/22% boost on DABStep easy score compared with base/scaffolded model:.

We can also see, that the hard score can increase too even though our dataset is focused on easier questions:.

From figures above one can notice a noticeable impact of both new scaffolding and tuning on our synthetic notebooks. This makes Qwen-4B (with our pipeline + scaffolding) a state-of-the-art small-model agent on DABStep.

In practice, the model can now solve a wide range of realistic Kaggle-style data analysis tasks with consistent execution.It’s not yet strong enough for the hardest queries, but we’ve shown that even small models can become powerful agents when paired with the right data and scaffolding.

These results demonstrate that even small models can become powerful data science agents with the right training approach. Ready to try it yourself? We've made everything openly available so you can experiment with our fine-tuned models and dataset.

We openly release best-performing checkpoints of tuned Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 together with the training dataset, which you can try out and experiment with:.

Maybe this will lead to… Jupyter-Agent 3. 😉.

We hope that our findings will inspire others to continue progress in developing more powerful notebook coding agents and we're excited to see what the community builds next. Dive into our jupyter-agent dataset on the 🤗 Hub and explore the codebase at https://github.com/huggingface/jupyter-agent to start your own experiments on agents for jupyter notebooks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
  • A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.
  • The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

It has been revealed that “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the organization had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”.

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment claims the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

Recent findings suggest that the government stated Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim tech giant that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

Recent findings suggest that the following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme noted RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”.

According to recent reports, A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”.

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme remarked RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

In a recent development, A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

Sources indicate that but Ihme said a review of the tech giant’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

Recent findings suggest that A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

Industry observers note that “The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme remarked. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”.

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit rapidly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

According to recent reports, the Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”.

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a fresh negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

According to recent reports, “I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”.

Recent findings suggest that ihme noted RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the tech giant’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

Recent findings suggest that “If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”.

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

It has been revealed that around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

Sources indicate that in July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#80916. Latest Update: The Cell, Not the Team: Three Roles That Make One Engineer Accountable

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2267 w)
